\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}

We study lead-lag analysis pitfalls in iterative training collapse using Pythia-410M \cite{biderman2023pythia}, a 410M-parameter decoder-only language model.
Pythia provides a controlled setting: small enough for multi-seed experiments across six contamination levels, yet large enough to exhibit meaningful generation-over-generation degradation.
Cross-architecture validation uses GPT-2-medium (345M parameters, also decoder-only), a second transformer family of similar scale; results are reported in \S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}, \S\ref{sec:regime}, and \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
Training data is drawn from WikiText-103 \cite{merity2017pointer}, using 5{,}000-sample subsets per generation.

Our protocol follows the replace paradigm of \citet{shumailov2024curse}, adapted for mixed synthetic-real training at $\alpha{<}1.0$.
Each generation $t$ proceeds in three steps: (1)~fine-tune the generation-$(t{-}1)$ model for 5{,}000 steps on a mixture of $\alpha$ fraction synthetic data and $(1{-}\alpha)$ fraction real data (AdamW optimizer, learning rate $5 \times 10^{-5}$, 500 warmup steps, weight decay $0.01$, batch size 4 for Pythia-410M, 32 for GPT-2-medium); (2)~generate 5{,}000 synthetic samples from the fine-tuned model (temperature $1.0$, top-$k{=}50$, max length 512 tokens); (3)~fully replace the synthetic pool.
We run $T{=}10$ generations (11 time points including the generation-0 baseline) across contamination levels $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00\}$.
The $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition uses four random seeds $\{42, 43, 44, 45\}$; $\alpha \in \{0.00, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75\}$ each use three seeds $\{42, 43, 44\}$; $\alpha{=}0.10$ uses a single seed (42, preliminary).

We track two \emph{canary metrics} (cheap-to-compute statistics hypothesized to precede downstream degradation, inspired by early-warning signals in dynamical systems \cite{scheffer2009early}) and three \emph{downstream metrics}.
Canary metrics are token entropy (next-token prediction entropy averaged over held-out samples) and expected calibration error (ECE).
Downstream metrics are distinct-1 and distinct-2 ($n$-gram diversity \cite{li2016diversity}, computed over all 5{,}000 generated samples per generation) and perplexity (evaluated on held-out real data).
Token entropy is the mean next-token prediction entropy $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ averaged over 1{,}000 held-out samples; ECE uses 15 equal-width bins.
We additionally evaluate effective rank and Self-BLEU as candidate canaries (\S\ref{sec:case_study}).
Results for distinct-3 are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}.
Code and data will be released upon publication.

All hypothesis tests apply Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$.
Permutation Granger causality tests use 5{,}000 permutations on first-differenced series \cite{shojaie2022granger}.
Cross-correlation analysis uses a maximum lag of 5 generations.
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} summarizes raw metric drift from generation~0 to generation~10 across all six contamination levels.

\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:method_sensitivity}

We open with Claim~3 (method sensitivity) because it conditions the interpretation of all subsequent results.
If different statistical methods yield contradictory conclusions on the same data, any single-method analysis is unreliable by construction.

\paragraph{Five-method ablation.}
We apply five lead-lag detection methods to the $\alpha{=}1.0$ condition (4~seeds, 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs).
The fraction of pairs reaching BH-corrected FDR significance varies dramatically by method: naive cross-correlation \textbf{16/16} (100\%), differenced cross-correlation \textbf{14/16} (87.5\%), threshold onset detection \textbf{9/16} (56.3\%), permutation Granger causality \textbf{6/16} (37.5\%), and Toda--Yamamoto Granger \textbf{5/16} (31.3\%; moderate supplementary, \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Method choice alone swings significance from \textbf{100\% to 37.5\%} among the primary methods: 50--57\% of pairs classified as significant under one method flip to non-significant under another.
The spurious-signal rate (the fraction of pairs detected by the most liberal method but not confirmed by the most conservative) is at least \textbf{62.5\%} across the primary methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reports significance rates restricted to 8 validated canary$\to$downstream pairs (excluding failed candidates); the 16-pair rates above include effective rank and Self-BLEU to capture the full method-sensitivity landscape.

\paragraph{First-differencing diagnostic.}
A single preprocessing decision can eliminate an entire analysis channel.
For canary$\to$diversity pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$, all pairs retain unanimous FDR significance after first-differencing (24/24$\to$24/24), confirming genuine temporal precedence rather than shared-trend confounding.
For canary$\to$perplexity, however, undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find \textbf{zero} significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$; Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}a).
The apparent canary$\to$perplexity relationship is entirely an artifact of co-trending.
Notably, at $\alpha{=}0.75$, differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions per seed, demonstrating that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics even after detrending.

\paragraph{Augmentation order sensitivity.}
Toda--Yamamoto Granger tests show extreme sensitivity to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b).
After correcting the statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$) at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$; however, the qualitative finding that this single hyperparameter can swing conclusions between near-universal significance and near-universal non-significance remains, consistent with known properties of the Toda--Yamamoto procedure~\cite{toda1995statistical}.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/differencing_dmax.pdf}
\caption{First-differencing diagnostic and augmentation order sensitivity (Pythia-410M, $\alpha{=}1.0$, 4~seeds). \textbf{(a)}~First-differencing eliminates the canary$\to$perplexity channel: undifferenced tests find near-universal significance ($F{=}16$--$36$) while differenced tests find zero significant pairs ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$), exposing these associations as shared-trend artifacts. Canary$\to$diversity pairs retain significance after differencing (24/24$\to$24/24). \textbf{(b)}~Toda--Yamamoto Granger significance rates vary dramatically with augmentation order $d_{\max}$; after correcting the implementation (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), TY achieves moderate detection at the default $d_{\max}{=}1$, but the qualitative sensitivity to this hyperparameter persists.}
\label{fig:differencing_dmax}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Inter-method agreement.}
Cohen's $\kappa$, averaged over all method pairs, is \textbf{0.185} (near chance; poor agreement); this value is consistent across contamination levels ($\alpha{=}0.0$ through $\alpha{=}1.0$), indicating that method disagreement is a structural property of the analysis rather than a regime-specific artifact.
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium (12 canary$\to$downstream pairs) yields Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$, also in the ``slight agreement'' range, confirming that low inter-method agreement is not architecture-specific.
Restricting to three informative methods (excluding naive cross-correlation, which anchors the permissive extreme, and Toda--Yamamoto, which provides moderate supplementary signal) raises $\kappa$ to 0.667 (substantial agreement), indicating that the low full-panel $\kappa$ is driven by the deliberate inclusion of methods spanning the entire permissive-to-conservative spectrum rather than by fundamental incoherence among methods.
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} extends the analysis across contamination levels.
Direction checking (D111) itself constitutes a sensitivity dimension beyond the five statistical methods: restricting to forward-direction associations inverts naive cross-correlation's profile from uniformly high (${\approx}100\%$ undirected) to regime-dependent, revealing that much of its apparent signal was reverse-directional.
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (null control), naive cross-correlation still finds \textbf{75\%} (6/8) of forward-direction pairs significant---lower than the undirected 100\%, but still a substantial FPR.
Permutation Granger correctly finds 0\%, achieving perfect null-control specificity.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), permutation Granger finds 75\% (6/8), while naive finds 37.5\% (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}; Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).

\paragraph{Method$\times$regime interaction.}
Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison} reveals that direction checking reshapes the method hierarchy across contamination levels.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, naive cross-correlation drops to 12.5\% while permutation Granger remains at 0\%, narrowing the gap visible in undirected analysis.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, naive rises to 87.5\% while permutation Granger reaches 75\%; both methods detect, but naive's persistent 75\% null-control FPR means its high-$\alpha$ detections cannot be distinguished from false positives without the consensus framework.
This regime-dependent reversal, combined with the block structure visible in Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap}, motivates the regime-dependent analysis in \S\ref{sec:regime}.

\paragraph{Why permutation Granger succeeds.}
The systematic comparison identifies PermG as the only method combining zero null-control FPR with consistent detection across all regimes where signal exists ($\alpha{\geq}0.50$).
Three properties explain this outcome.
First, the nonparametric permutation procedure inherently controls FPR by constructing the null distribution from the observed data rather than from distributional assumptions, making it robust to the non-stationarity that inflates false positives in correlation-based methods.
Second, Granger tests are directional by construction: they test whether past values of $X$ improve prediction of $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history, naturally filtering the reverse-directional associations that inflate naive cross-correlation's FPR.
Third, PermG does not require threshold calibration or augmentation order selection, avoiding the hyperparameter sensitivity observed in Toda--Yamamoto (Figure~\ref{fig:differencing_dmax}b; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}) and the power limitations that reduce threshold onset to near-zero detection under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}).
By contrast, differenced cross-correlation retains 100\% FDR significance in both forward \emph{and} reverse directions at $\alpha{=}0.75$, failing to distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics; and Toda--Yamamoto, while achieving moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
These complementary failures, exposed through the MMCT evaluation framework, converge on a single recommendation: for short iterative training series ($T{\leq}20$), permutation Granger causality should be the primary detection method.

\subsection{Regime-Dependent Detectability}
\label{sec:regime}

Beyond method choice, the contamination level~$\alpha$ determines whether a temporal lead exists to detect.
We present regime effects at two levels: raw metric drift (method-independent) and Granger-precedence detectability.

\paragraph{Raw drift.}
Table~\ref{tab:drift_summary} shows that diversity collapse occurs at \emph{all} contamination levels, not only under full synthetic replacement.
Distinct-1 declines by 13.8\% even at $\alpha{=}0.0$ (attributable to fine-tuning on repeated real-data subsets).
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ reveals a steep diversity cliff: distinct-1 drops by 39.6\%, nearly matching the 3-seed mean at $\alpha{=}0.25$ ($-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$); distinct-2 shows a comparable jump ($-56.4\%$ vs.\ $-56.4{\pm}0.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.25$).
Token entropy at $\alpha{=}0.10$, however, differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$), constituting a canary blind spot in which diversity has already collapsed but no canary metric responds.
At higher contamination, distinct-1 decline continues: $-37.1{\pm}0.4\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.50$), $-32.3{\pm}0.5\%$ ($\alpha{=}0.75$), and $-27.8{\pm}1.6\%$ ($\alpha{=}1.0$).
The non-monotonic pattern (diversity declining \emph{more} at moderate~$\alpha$ than at extreme~$\alpha$) is confirmed by 3-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (std${=}0.3\%$), indicating that this relationship between contamination level and collapse severity is robust rather than a seed-specific artifact.

\paragraph{Granger-precedence detectability.}
Despite ubiquitous drift, causal detectability is sharply regime-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}).
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced, BH-corrected) find 0/8 pairs FDR-significant from $\alpha{=}0.00$ through $\alpha{=}0.45$ (including $\alpha{=}0.25$ where a faint single-pair signal appears at FDR $p{=}0.053$ but aggregate detection remains null, and $\alpha{=}0.35$/$0.40$/$0.45$ which confirm PermG fwd${=}$0/8), \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (2~fp32 seeds, consistent), \textbf{3/8} and \textbf{0/8} at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (s42 and s43 respectively; dual-seed confirmed non-monotonic dip), and \textbf{6/8} at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
At $\alpha{=}0.75$ (3~seeds), permutation Granger finds 20/24 forward-direction pairs FDR-significant with 0/24 reverse, confirming directional asymmetry; however, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds), placing this regime in a transitional detection state.
Under Bonferroni correction, approximately 3/8 pairs per seed survive, consistent with the transitional nature of the $\alpha{=}0.75$ boundary where marginal signals are sensitive to correction stringency.
Within-$\alpha$ multi-seed analysis at $\alpha{=}1.0$ yields \textbf{24/24} canary$\to$diversity pairs FDR-significant across all four seeds, with 0/24 in the reverse direction, confirming temporal asymmetry.
Permutation Granger forward significance is the primary detection indicator (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}): it reaches 6/8 at $\alpha{=}0.50$, dips to 3/8 at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (synchronous collapse zone; see below), and recovers to 5--6/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
The onset boundary lies at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$: finer-grained probing at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$ yields PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at all three levels, extending the blind spot through $\alpha{=}0.45$.
A faint signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (best-pair FDR $p{=}0.053$) but does not translate to aggregate detection; reliable detection begins at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, 2~seeds).
This sharp phase transition is consistent with theoretical expectations about signal-to-noise limits in short time series~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
Sensitivity analysis confirms that treatment/null separation is robust to FDR threshold choice ($q{=}0.01$: 0/24 null, 0/24 treatment at $\alpha{=}0.75$; $q{=}0.10$: 0/24 null, 24/24 treatment; Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
Cross-architecture validation on GPT-2-medium confirms this boundary: at $\alpha{=}0.25$, at most 1/8 pairs reach $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$), consistent with the null regime, despite substantially stronger canary drift (entropy $-32.8\%$ vs.\ Pythia $-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$), while at $\alpha{=}1.0$ all 6 canary$\to$diversity pairs reach significance (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime} summarizes the regime map across both architectures.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 1/8 pairs at Tier~3 ($K{\geq}4/5$) and 7/8 at Tier~2 ($K{\geq}3/5$), consistent with Pythia's 0/8 Tier~3, 0/8 Tier~2 result at the same contamination level, placing both architectures in the null/low-detectability regime.

\paragraph{Detectability at $\alpha{=}0.50$ and the transition zone.}
Under fp32 precision, $\alpha{=}0.50$ is reliably detected: permutation Granger finds 6/8 pairs FDR-significant across both seeds (Table~\ref{tab:method_comparison}).
The transition from undetectable to reliably detectable occurs between $\alpha{=}0.45$ and $\alpha{=}0.50$: finer-grained probing confirms PermG fwd${=}$0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.35$, $0.40$, and $0.45$, while $\alpha{=}0.50$ achieves 6/8 (2~seeds).
A faint single-pair signal first appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (entropy$\to$distinct-1: raw $p{=}0.007$, FDR-corrected $p{=}0.053$), but all aggregate indicators remain null through $\alpha{=}0.45$, placing the onset boundary at $\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$, canary sensitivity remains metric-dependent: ECE achieves significance in both fp32 seeds, while token entropy remains below the FDR threshold ($p_{\text{fdr}}{\geq}0.086$), identifying ECE as the more sensitive canary near the onset boundary.
Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_heatmap} visualizes the method$\times\alpha$ interaction, revealing a block structure that separates correlation-based methods from causal methods as a function of regime.

\paragraph{Non-monotonic dose-response: the synchronous collapse zone.}
Dual-seed replication at $\alpha{=}0.60$ reveals a non-monotonic dose-response in Granger detectability: PermG fwd drops to 3/8 (s42) and 0/8 (s43), below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ (6/8, 2~seeds) and $\alpha{=}0.75$ (5--6/8 per seed, 3~seeds).
This creates a four-regime structure in the dose-response profile: \emph{blind spot} ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$, 0/8), \emph{onset} ($\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$), \emph{synchronous collapse} ($\alpha{\approx}0.60$, 0--3/8), and \emph{detection zone} ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$, 5--8/8).
The dip is inconsistent with a monotonically increasing signal-to-noise model; we hypothesize that at $\alpha{=}0.60$, canary and downstream metrics respond to contamination simultaneously rather than sequentially, destroying the temporal lead that Granger tests require (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind spot, canary drift is indistinguishable from the null; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream metrics drift substantially but without temporal offset.
Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection across this range (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with its detection at $\alpha{=}0.60$ suggesting partial inter-method complementarity in the synchronous collapse zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8.
This non-monotonicity also implies that simple threshold-based triggers (such as the 15\% entropy criterion in \S\ref{sec:intervention}) may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.


\subsection{Case Study: Canary Prediction of Diversity Collapse}
\label{sec:case_study}

Having established method sensitivity (Claim~3) and regime dependence (Claim~2), we present the conditions under which canary prediction succeeds (Claim~1).
We scope this claim precisely: canary metrics predict \emph{diversity collapse} (declining distinct-$n$), not model collapse broadly.

\paragraph{Full synthetic replacement ($\alpha{=}1.0$, 4 seeds).}
Token entropy exhibits robust Granger-precedence over diversity collapse metrics, confirmed by 4 independent statistical methods (permutation Granger power${=}1.0$), 4 seeds, and cross-architecture replication on GPT-2-medium (Tier~3 consensus; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Cross-correlation peaks at lag$={+}1$ with $|r|{>}0.99$ (cross-seed standard deviation: 0.0), establishing a consistent one-generation lead.
Figure~\ref{fig:metric_trajectory} illustrates the one-generation offset between token entropy decline and distinct-1 decline, visible across all four seeds.
Permutation Granger tests (first-differenced) confirm all canary$\to$diversity pairs as FDR-significant across all four seeds, including distinct-3 (Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3}).
Reverse-direction tests (downstream$\to$canary) on WikiText-103 find \textbf{0/24} FDR-significant (all $p{>}0.49$), establishing directional asymmetry in this domain.\footnote{C4 exhibits domain-dependent directionality: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}

\paragraph{High contamination ($\alpha{=}0.75$, 3 seeds).}
Directional asymmetry is robustly confirmed across three independent seeds (permutation Granger: 20/24 forward pairs FDR-significant, 0/24 reverse).
However, method-level consensus varies by seed (Tier~3 pairs: 4, 3, and 1 across seeds 42, 43, 44), placing $\alpha{=}0.75$ squarely in the transitional detection regime.
Differenced cross-correlation finds 8/8 pairs significant in \emph{both} forward and reverse directions at each seed, confirming that this method alone cannot distinguish genuine directional precedence from shared dynamics, a seed-level demonstration of Pitfall~1 (\S\ref{sec:pitfalls}).

\paragraph{ECE as a conditional secondary canary.}
ECE's forward consensus matches token entropy (both achieve PermG\_fwd 6/8 across all conditions), but the reverse profile diverges sharply.
Across 7 validated conditions at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (3 architectures $\times$ 2 scales $\times$ 2 domains), token entropy reverse direction yields \textbf{0/28} FDR-significant pairs (consistent with unidirectional forward causation at full synthetic replacement; domain-dependent bidirectionality emerges at lower $\alpha$, \S\ref{sec:discussion}), while ECE reverse direction yields \textbf{13/28} significant pairs, with 5/7 conditions containing at least one reverse-significant pair, all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction.
This bidirectional coupling is the core reason ECE is classified as a secondary canary: ECE and diversity exhibit mutual feedback, and the interpretability of ECE's causal direction is correspondingly limited.
This result also instantiates Claim~3 (method sensitivity): when only forward significance is considered, the two canary types appear equivalent; incorporating reverse-direction tests separates them. The choice of analysis dimension alters the canary classification itself.

\paragraph{Failed canary candidates.}
Not all metrics serve as canaries.
Effective rank and Self-BLEU show no detectable lead-lag relationship with any downstream metric under any method or contamination level, and are excluded from the consensus framework.
Effective rank behavior is model-dependent in an unexpected way: in Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases during collapse (representational contraction), whereas in GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$ it \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The GPT-2-medium starting effective rank is near rank-2, suggesting the model's initial representation is already highly concentrated; iterative training disperses it rather than concentrating it further.
This opposite directionality across architectures precludes effective rank as a universal canary and motivates architecture-specific analysis (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Consensus filtering.}
Of 16 canary$\to$downstream pairs tested at $\alpha{=}1.0$ (4 candidate canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics), \textbf{6 survive} the full consensus pipeline (PermG fwd ${\geq}6/8$, $S{\geq}3/4$ seeds): token entropy and ECE each predicting distinct-1 and distinct-2 (4 pairs; distinct-3 results in Appendix~\ref{app:distinct3} bring the total to~6).
The 10 eliminated pairs comprise all canary$\to$perplexity relationships (identified as spurious by the first-differencing diagnostic) and all effective-rank and Self-BLEU pairs (failed canaries).
The consensus framework reduces the naive 75\% forward-direction FPR to 0\%, matching the most conservative individual methods (Figure~\ref{fig:consensus_workflow}).


\subsection{Consensus Framework Validation}
\label{sec:consensus_validation}

We validate the consensus framework's calibration using built-in experimental controls.

\paragraph{False positive rate.}
At $\alpha{=}0.0$ (three seeds, 24 total pairs), no synthetic data is injected; any detected lead-lag association is a false positive.
Individual-method forward-direction FPR ranges from \textbf{75\%} (naive cross-correlation: 6/8) through 37.5\% (threshold) down to \textbf{0\%} (permutation Granger and differenced cross-correlation); Toda--Yamamoto's null-control FPR has not yet been evaluated through the corrected pipeline (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
The multi-method consensus at $K{\geq}3$ ($3\sigma$) achieves \textbf{FPR${=}$0\%} (0/24 pairs, three independent seeds), matching the best individual method (permutation Granger) while providing a formal benchmark for method reliability (Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr}).

\paragraph{False negative rate.}
At $\alpha{=}1.0$, we define 6 effect-size reference pairs (token entropy and ECE $\to$ distinct-1/2/3) using criteria independent of the consensus methods: drift ratio ${\geq}3\times$ the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline (entropy $11.93\times$, ECE $73.12\times$) and canary onset strictly preceding downstream onset by ${\geq}1$ generation (\S\ref{sec:calibration}).
FNR is calibrated on a 4-method panel (excluding differenced cross-correlation to avoid circularity): at $K{\geq}3/4$, $S{\geq}3/4$, all~6 are recovered (\textbf{FNR${=}$0\%}).
Toda--Yamamoto's individual FNR is 50\% (4/8 detected at $\alpha{=}1.0$, seed~42), consistent with its moderate supplementary classification (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Both FPR and FNR are validated on the joint method${\times}$seed dimension (FPR: 3~seeds at $\alpha{=}0.0$; FNR: 4~seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$), with cross-seed FPR variance negligible (all three seeds yield 0/8 robust pairs at $K{\geq}3$).
Table~\ref{tab:fpr_fnr} reports the calibration results.
Table~\ref{tab:single-method-errors} complements this analysis by showing the practical consequences of relying on any single method: naive cross-correlation produces false positives at every $\alpha$ including the null control, while permutation Granger achieves correct verdicts at all levels with zero FPR.

\paragraph{Bootstrap power analysis.}
To quantify detection power beyond binary FNR, we perform bootstrap power analysis ($B{=}1{,}000$ resamples from 4-seed data at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
Permutation Granger achieves power${=}1.0$ on genuine pairs (canary$\to$diversity) and power${=}0.0$ on spurious pairs (canary$\to$perplexity), providing clean separation.
Toda--Yamamoto achieves power${=}0.50$ on genuine pairs (4/8 detected at $\alpha{=}1.0$), consistent with its moderate supplementary classification (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
We note that bootstrap power${=}1.0$ reflects the effect size in our 4-seed data and should not be interpreted as a universal power guarantee; furthermore, the two methods use different data-generating processes for calibration (permutation Granger resamples observed $\alpha{=}1.0$ trajectories, while Toda--Yamamoto power was estimated under a generic VAR(2) simulation with $\beta{=}0.3$).

\multicolumn{6}{l}{\footnotesize Full method-level breakdown ($K{\geq}4$) in Appendix~\ref{app:cross_arch}.} \\
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Cross-condition robustness.}
Table~\ref{tab:generalization} confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern is robust across 14 confirmed conditions (3 pending) spanning six model families (Pythia, GPT-2, OPT, Qwen, SmolLM3, Padding-variant), scales from 345M to 6.9B, and two training domains (WikiText-103, C4).
Permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 12 of 14 conditions (85.7\%), with two exceptions: Pythia-1.4B seed~42 (2/8), a seed-dependent outlier that recovers to 6/8 in seed~43, and SmolLM3-3B (3/8), where only ECE$\to$downstream pairs are detected (see below).
$K{\geq}3$ multi-method consensus reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 conditions (11/14 pending Padding-410M audit), with exceptions Pythia-1.4B (s42: 1/8, s43: 3/8) and SmolLM3-3B (3/8).
The concordance between PermG and $K{\geq}3$ confirms that multi-method consensus is robust across architectures.
With threshold onset power-limited and Toda--Yamamoto providing moderate supplementary signal (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$; \S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), $K{\geq}3$ draws on four contributing methods---a stronger standard than simple majority (\S\ref{sec:consensus}).

\paragraph{Scale generalization.}
Scaling from 410M to 6.9B parameters confirms that the lead-lag pattern persists across a $17\times$ parameter range.
Pythia-6.9B achieves PermG fwd~7/8 (bf16), the strongest single-seed detection.
Within the Pythia family, 1.4B shows seed dependence: s42 yields only 2/8 (the sole outlier across all conditions), while s43 recovers to 6/8.
Qwen3.5-0.8B (PermG~fwd~8/8) extends the finding beyond the Pythia/GPT-2/OPT decoder-only family to an independently trained architecture with a different tokenizer.

\paragraph{Domain generalization.}
Replacing WikiText-103 with C4 yields the strongest forward detection: Pythia-1B achieves PermG~fwd~8/8 in both seeds at $\alpha{=}1.0$, confirming that the lead-lag pattern is not an artifact of narrow topical distribution.
However, directional asymmetry does not transfer fully across domains.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Pythia-410M, C4, s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8 (compared to 0/8 in all WikiText conditions), indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling between canary and downstream metrics.
This domain-dependent directionality suggests that the unidirectional forward causation observed in WikiText may partly reflect domain-specific dynamics rather than a universal property of collapse; implications are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

\paragraph{Canary metric sensitivity: the SmolLM3-3B case.}
\label{sec:smollm3}
SmolLM3-3B (PermG fwd 3/8) reveals that canary metric choice is itself a dimension of method sensitivity.
Decomposing by canary type: ECE$\to$downstream achieves 3/4 significant pairs, while token entropy$\to$downstream achieves 0/4.
The root cause is that SmolLM3's token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations, violating the monotonic decline pattern that Granger tests exploit; ECE, by contrast, maintains its monotonic upward trajectory.
Multi-method consensus confirms the severity: entropy pairs activate only via naive and differenced cross-correlation (per-pair $K{=}2$), ECE pairs activate only via differenced cross-correlation and permutation Granger (per-pair $K{=}2$), and no pair exceeds two-method agreement---illustrating that even within a single architecture, the method panel fragments along canary metric boundaries.
This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal across all architectures, enriching Claim~3 by adding canary metric selection as a further source of analytic variability.

\subsection{Canary-Based Early Intervention}
\label{sec:intervention}

To test whether the lead-lag relationship translates into practical utility, we implement a predictive cessation protocol: training with synthetic data ($\alpha{=}1.0$) continues until token entropy drops ${>}15\%$ relative to generation~0, at which point $\alpha$ is switched to $0.0$ (pure real data).
We compare against a reactive baseline that triggers only when distinct-1 drops ${>}10\%$---a downstream metric that, by the lead-lag hypothesis, should respond later.

\paragraph{Pythia-410M.}
The predictive trigger fires at generation~1 in both seed-precision pairs tested (s42 fp32: entropy $3.234{\to}1.918$, ${\downarrow}40.7\%$; s43 bf16: $3.257{\to}2.523$, ${\downarrow}22.5\%$).
The reactive baseline triggers one generation later (generation~2, distinct-1 ${\downarrow}15.6\%$).
Predictive intervention reduces peak perplexity by 63\% relative to reactive ($56.99$ vs.\ $157.09$, s42 fp32) and achieves full recovery by generation~2 versus generation~4 for reactive.
The bf16 pair shows a milder perturbation (peak perplexity $24.65$ vs.\ $56.99$) consistent with stochastic rounding regularization, but the structural pattern---generation~1 trigger, generation~2 recovery---is identical.
Both conditions converge to the $\alpha{=}0.0$ baseline by generation~10.

\paragraph{Cross-scale validation: Pythia-1.4B.}
Pythia-1.4B (s42 fp32) replicates the 410M pattern: token entropy drops $51.9\%$ at generation~1 ($2.946{\to}1.418$), exceeding the 15\% threshold, and recovers to $2.892$ by generation~2 ($98.2\%$ of baseline).
Perplexity spikes from $19.68$ to $65.37$ at the trigger generation and recovers to $17.44$ by generation~2 (stable at $17.60$ through generation~10).
The trigger generation, recovery timeline, and convergence behavior are identical across the $3.4\times$ scale gap (410M to 1.4B), confirming that the canary-based intervention mechanism is scale-independent: the 15\% entropy threshold generalizes without recalibration across model sizes.

75	\paragraph{Canary metric choice as a sensitivity dimension.}
76	SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a dimension of method sensitivity beyond the five statistical methods analyzed in Claim~3.
77	Token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations in SmolLM3, violating the monotonic decline assumed by Granger tests and producing 0/4 significant entropy$\to$downstream pairs.
78	ECE, by contrast, maintains monotonic growth and achieves 3/4 significant pairs (PermG fwd: 3/8 overall).
79	The two canary types activate through partially disjoint method subsets: entropy pairs reach significance via naive and differenced cross-correlation, while ECE pairs reach significance via differenced cross-correlation and permutation Granger.

83	
84	\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
85	The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
86	At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
87	At $\alpha{\leq}0.45$, where early warning would be most valuable, aggregate canary detection remains null (a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ but does not reach aggregate detection through $\alpha{=}0.45$).
88	A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
89	This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
90	At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
91	This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
92	At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
93	This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
94	The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
95	If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.
96	
97	\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
98	In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
99	A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
100	The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
101	The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.
102	
103	\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
104	Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
105	This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
106	Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), validated across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, provide cross-scale evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
107	Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
108	Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
109	These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
110	The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.
111	
112	\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
113	In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
114	Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
115	The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
116	The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the scope of intervention validation (three seed-precision pairs across two model scales at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment---particularly to larger models and accumulate-mode training---requires further confirmation.
117	The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; notably, the threshold trigger fires at $\alpha{=}0.60$ even though formal Granger detection fails at this level (synchronous collapse zone; \S\ref{sec:regime}), illustrating that magnitude-based triggers can complement temporal-precedence tests.
118	However, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.
119	
120	\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
121	The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
122	The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
123	The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
124	In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
125	First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
126	Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.
127	
128	\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
129	Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
130	First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
131	This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods; Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection (3--4/8) at $T{=}11$ reflects this constraint, as the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ consumes additional degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
132	Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
133	Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
134	Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
135	These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.
136	
137	\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
138	We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
139	TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
140	This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
141	The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
142	This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.
143	
144	Change-point analysis under the null condition ($\alpha{=}0.00$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
145	Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary$\to$downstream significance (24/24) while eliminating reverse-direction signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).
146	
147	\paragraph{Future work.}
148	Several directions extend this work.
149	Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
150	Multi-seed replication across the six validated architecture families would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}7$B parameters) remains an open direction.

152	The SmolLM3 finding (ECE-only detection due to non-monotonic entropy) motivates systematic study of which canary metric is most reliable per architecture family.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Granger precedence is not causation.}
Granger causality tests whether past values of one series improve prediction of another beyond its own history; it does not establish true causation~\cite{granger1969investigating,shojaie2022granger}.
Bivariate Granger tests cannot exclude confounders: an unobserved process (such as a latent distributional shift in the training data) could independently drive both token entropy and diversity metrics, producing spurious lead-lag associations even when no direct relationship exists.
Our multi-method consensus framework inherits this limitation in full.
Throughout this paper, ``Granger precedence'' denotes predictive improvement in a time-series forecasting sense, not a causal mechanism.
This distinction is why we scope our central claim to ``token entropy Granger-precedes diversity collapse'' rather than asserting that token entropy \emph{causes} diversity collapse.

\paragraph{Calibration scope and generalization.}
All FPR and FNR calibration results reported in this work are specific to our experimental setup: Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia}, a WikiText-103 subset, $T{=}10$ generation cycles, and six contamination levels ($\alpha \in \{0.0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.0\}$).
Generalization to other model architectures, datasets, or training protocols requires independent validation.
The consensus framework's structure (multi-method agreement combined with multi-seed replication) is intended to be applicable beyond this specific setting, but the operating thresholds are empirically calibrated and may require re-tuning under different conditions.
For instance, architectures with different tokenizer granularity or training dynamics could shift the balance between false positive and false negative rates.
Cross-architecture validation across 14 confirmed conditions spanning six model families confirms that the entropy-leads-diversity pattern generalizes: permutation Granger forward significance reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 12 of 14 architecture-seed combinations (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}); SmolLM3-3B (3/8) diverges due to canary metric splitting (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
$K{\geq}3$ multi-method consensus reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 conditions (11/14 pending Padding-410M audit), confirming that multi-method agreement generalizes beyond the calibration setup; Pythia-1.4B (s42: 1/8, s43: 3/8) and SmolLM3-3B (3/8) reflect scale-dependent seed sensitivity and canary metric splitting rather than framework failure.
Reverse-direction tests at $\alpha{=}1.0$ reveal a canary-specific asymmetry: token entropy exhibits 0/28 reverse significance across all 7 validated conditions (consistent with unidirectional Granger precedence at full synthetic replacement), while ECE shows 13/28 reverse-significant pairs (5/7 conditions), all in the distinct$\to$ECE direction. This pattern confirms bidirectional feedback between calibration and diversity.
The unidirectionality of token entropy is domain-dependent: at $\alpha{=}0.50$ on C4 (s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8, indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling absent from all WikiText conditions at any contamination level (see below).
GPT-2-medium seed~43 exhibits the most pronounced bidirectional coupling: PermG reverse reaches 4/8, the highest of any condition, yet the forward signal (6/8) still exceeds the reverse, preserving net directionality.
Under extreme collapse ($\alpha{=}1.0$), the mutual feedback between diversity loss and calibration drift can strengthen the reverse channel without eliminating the forward lead, consistent with a model in which diversity collapse feeds back into calibration but does so with a lag that preserves the temporal ordering established in the forward direction.
Full-panel inter-method agreement remains low (Fleiss' $\kappa{=}0.091$) but rises to $\kappa{=}0.667$ among the three informative methods (\S\ref{sec:method_sensitivity}), confirming that the consensus framework's structure transfers across architectures even if operating thresholds require architecture-specific calibration.
At $\alpha{=}0.25$, GPT-2-medium yields 0/8 pairs at PermG fwd significance, placing it in the same null regime as Pythia and confirming that the detectability boundary is consistent across architectures.
The full GPT-2-medium drift profile at $\alpha{=}0.25$ is: entropy $-32.8\%$, ECE $+422\%$, perplexity $-44.5\%$, distinct-1 $-23.5\%$, distinct-2 $-31.6\%$, distinct-3 $-30.2\%$, MAUVE $0.0315 \to 0.0282$ ($-10.5\%$).
Compared to Pythia ($-4.7{\pm}0.5\%$ entropy, $-40.3{\pm}0.3\%$ distinct-1), GPT-2-medium shows substantially stronger canary drift but milder diversity decline, likely due to its $8\times$ larger batch size exposing more data per step.
The stronger canary signal approaches detectability (permutation Granger $F{=}64.09$, $p{=}0.081$ for entropy$\to$distinct-1, compared to $p{>}0.5$ in Pythia), suggesting that the regime boundary may shift with increased effective sample size, but single-seed $T{=}10$ power remains insufficient for Confirmatory claims.
Toda--Yamamoto Granger achieves 0/8 at $\alpha{=}0.25$ (consistent with the null regime) and moderate detection (3--4/8) only at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{From ad-hoc consensus to method recommendation.}
The primary value of the multi-method framework is not the consensus vote itself but the systematic comparison it enables.
By applying five methods with different inductive biases to the same data, the framework reveals \emph{why} each method succeeds or fails: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR because it captures reverse-directional associations; differenced cross-correlation cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence; threshold onset lacks power at $T{=}11$ under $3\sigma$ calibration (\S\ref{sec:threshold_limitation}); and Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8) but remains sensitive to the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
This process of elimination converges on permutation Granger as the recommended method: it is the only one combining zero null-control FPR, consistent detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$, and clean directional separation on WikiText (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
The MMCT weighted consensus (\S\ref{sec:mmct}) provides formal $p$-values grounded in the empirical null distribution, maintaining FPR${=}$0\%; however, the practical recommendation is simpler: for short iterative training series, permutation Granger alone provides reliable detection without requiring the full consensus machinery.
Multi-method consensus ($K{\geq}3$) remains useful as a robustness check, reaching ${\geq}6/8$ in 10 of 14 cross-architecture conditions (\S\ref{sec:generalization}), but threshold onset is power-limited and Toda--Yamamoto provides moderate supplementary signal (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), with four contributing methods supporting the $K{\geq}3$ threshold.

\paragraph{Short time-series constraint.}
With $T{=}10$ generation cycles (11 data points per series), our time-series analyses operate near the lower bound of what standard methods require.
This series length is typical for iterative training studies, where each generation involves a complete training run, but it severely limits statistical power.
After correcting a statsmodels API incompatibility (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}), Toda--Yamamoto achieves moderate detection (3--4/8 at $\alpha{\geq}0.50$), confirming that its lower rates reflect genuine power limitations at $T{=}11$ rather than implementation error.
This finding aligns with \citet{boettiger2012limits}, who demonstrated that early-warning signals have limited detection power in short time series.
Longer generation chains would improve power for all methods but impose substantial computational cost; this trade-off between statistical power and compute budget is inherent to iterative training research and cannot be resolved by methodological improvements alone.
However, observation window sensitivity analysis provides reassurance: the $4/5$ consensus classification stabilizes at $T{\geq}5$, well below our observation window of $T{=}10$, with identical results from $T{=}5$ through $T{=}10$ (Appendix~\ref{app:window_sensitivity}).
After implementation correction, Toda--Yamamoto's window sensitivity is consistent with its moderate detection profile: TY consensus stabilizes at $T{\geq}6$, slightly later than the primary methods ($T{\geq}5$), reflecting the additional degrees of freedom consumed by the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).

\paragraph{Effective rank direction is model-dependent.}
Effective rank evolves in opposite directions across architectures during iterative training.
In Pythia-410M, effective rank decreases (representational contraction), consistent with mode collapse concentrating the output distribution into fewer dimensions.
In GPT-2-medium at $\alpha{=}0.25$, effective rank \emph{increases} from 2.37 to 8.48 (+258\%).
The likely explanation is starting-point dependence: GPT-2-medium begins near rank-2 (a highly concentrated initial representation), and iterative training disperses activation mass across more dimensions rather than concentrating it further.
This finding demonstrates that effective rank cannot serve as a direction-agnostic canary and that its trajectory must be interpreted relative to architecture-specific baselines.
We note this as a caveat on the generality of representational metrics as collapse indicators, even when the regime map (Table~\ref{tab:cross_arch_regime}) and lead-lag detectability are consistent across architectures.

\paragraph{Diversity--calibration dissociation.}
Diversity metrics and calibration metrics respond to synthetic contamination in qualitatively opposite directions across the $\alpha$ spectrum.
Diversity collapse (distinct-$n$ decline) is most severe at low contamination ($\alpha{=}0.25$: distinct-3 declines by $58.9{\pm}0.9\%$) and attenuates at higher levels ($\alpha{=}1.0$: $-30.5\%$), while calibration degradation (ECE) increases monotonically with $\alpha$ ($+51.7\%$ at $\alpha{=}0.0$ to $+3780\%$ at $\alpha{=}1.0$).
This dissociation underscores the need for multi-method analysis: the regime in which a metric degrades most severely ($\alpha{=}0.25$ for diversity) does not coincide with the regime in which its temporal lead is most detectable ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), and a single metric family cannot capture the full picture of iterative training degradation.

\paragraph{Synchronous collapse at $\alpha{=}0.60$.}
The non-monotonic dose-response at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (PermG fwd: s42 3/8, s43 0/8, below both $\alpha{=}0.50$ and $\alpha{=}0.75$; \S\ref{sec:regime}) challenges the assumption that detectability improves monotonically with contamination severity.
We hypothesize that at $\alpha{=}0.60$, the contamination intensity crosses a threshold where canary and downstream metrics respond simultaneously to the distributional shift, eliminating the one-generation temporal lead that Granger tests exploit.
At lower contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional perturbation is mild enough to affect predictive uncertainty before output diversity measurably declines.
At higher contamination ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the perturbation is severe enough that the canary's response is disproportionately fast, re-establishing temporal separation.
The synchronous zone is mechanistically distinct from the blind spot: in the blind spot ($\alpha{\leq}0.45$), canary drift is indistinguishable from the null or too weak for aggregate detection; in the synchronous zone, both canary and downstream drift substantially but without temporal offset.
This creates a four-regime structure---blind spot, onset, synchronous collapse, detection zone---rather than the two-regime detect/no-detect boundary assumed by simpler models.
Toda--Yamamoto maintains moderate detection (3--4/8) across the $\alpha{=}0.50$--$0.75$ range including the synchronous zone where PermG drops to 0--3/8, suggesting partial inter-method complementarity: TY's augmented VAR formulation may be less sensitive to the temporal synchronization that suppresses PermG's signal at $\alpha{=}0.60$.
The finding also has practical implications: simple threshold-based triggers (e.g., the 15\% entropy criterion) fire at $\alpha{=}0.60$ because they respond to magnitude rather than temporal structure, suggesting that threshold triggers may outperform formal Granger tests at intermediate contamination levels.

\paragraph{Domain-dependent directionality.}
The unidirectional forward causation observed consistently in WikiText experiments (PermG reverse${=}$0/8 across all contamination levels and seeds) does not hold universally.
On C4 at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (Pythia-410M, s42 fp32), PermG reverse reaches 7/8 (forward: 8/8), indicating near-symmetric bidirectional coupling between canary and downstream metrics (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
This stands in sharp contrast to the same model at the same contamination level on WikiText, where PermG reverse${=}$0/8.
One possible explanation is that C4's broader distributional characteristics (Common Crawl vs.\ encyclopedic Wikipedia text) alter the temporal dynamics of collapse: the richer distributional structure may allow downstream diversity metrics to feed back into canary metrics more quickly, shortening the temporal offset that WikiText's narrower distribution preserves.
Alternatively, the pre-training data confound (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) may play a role, since Pythia was pre-trained on the Pile which includes C4-overlapping data.
The practical implication is that directional asymmetry should be verified per domain rather than assumed to transfer from WikiText-based calibration; the forward detection itself (PermG fwd${=}$8/8) remains robust across both domains.

\paragraph{Canary metric choice as a sensitivity dimension.}
SmolLM3-3B reveals that canary metric selection constitutes a dimension of method sensitivity beyond the five statistical methods analyzed in Claim~3.
Token entropy exhibits non-monotonic oscillations across generations in SmolLM3, violating the monotonic decline assumed by Granger tests and producing 0/4 significant entropy$\to$downstream pairs.
ECE, by contrast, maintains monotonic growth and achieves 3/4 significant pairs (PermG fwd: 3/8 overall).
The two canary types activate through partially disjoint method subsets: entropy pairs reach significance via naive and differenced cross-correlation, while ECE pairs reach significance via differenced cross-correlation and permutation Granger.
SmolLM3-3B achieves $K{\geq}3$ = 3/8 (matching PermG fwd), confirming that consensus tracks individual-method detection even in this challenging case; however, the low overall detection (3/8) places SmolLM3 as one of three outliers ($K{\geq}3$ $<6/8$) across the 14-condition cross-architecture panel.
This architecture-dependent canary sensitivity complements the finding that effective rank direction is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:case_study}): no single canary metric is universally optimal.
The practical implication is that monitoring dashboards should track multiple canary candidates, adapting the active metric to the architecture under evaluation.

\paragraph{Practical utility paradox.}
The canary framework exhibits a paradox: it works best where it is least needed.
At $\alpha{\geq}0.75$, token entropy reliably Granger-precedes diversity collapse, but at these contamination levels degradation is already severe and likely detectable through simpler means.
At $\alpha{\leq}0.45$, where early warning would be most valuable, aggregate canary detection remains null (a faint single-pair signal appears at $\alpha{=}0.25$ but does not reach aggregate detection through $\alpha{=}0.45$).
A single-seed observation at $\alpha{=}0.10$ sharpens this limitation: distinct-1 already declines by 39.6\% (comparable to the multi-seed $\alpha{=}0.25$ result of $-40.3\%$), yet token entropy differs from the null by less than 1 percentage point ($-5.3\%$ vs.\ $-4.6{\pm}0.4\%$).
This canary blind spot means that even small amounts of synthetic contamination can trigger diversity collapse without activating any canary warning.
At $\alpha{=}0.50$ (fp32), detectability is reliable (PermG fwd: 6/8, both seeds consistent), with ECE outperforming token entropy as the more sensitive canary at this level.
This sensitivity difference reflects how each metric aggregates distributional information: ECE decomposes calibration error across multiple probability bins, making it responsive to changes in the shape of the predicted distribution rather than just its mean, while token entropy compresses the full distribution into a single scalar average.
At moderate contamination ($\alpha{=}0.50$), the distributional shifts are subtle enough that bin-level decomposition detects them but the global average does not.
This is not a framework deficiency but an inherent characteristic of collapse dynamics: at low contamination, diversity changes are too small relative to inter-generation noise for any temporal lead to emerge above the statistical detection floor~\cite{boettiger2012limits}.
The practical implication is that the framework is better suited to continuous monitoring dashboards that track metric trajectories across many generations than to single-point detection decisions.
If contamination grows over time (as in realistic web-scale data pipelines), the canary signal will strengthen as $\alpha$ increases, providing earlier detection than post-hoc quality audits.

\paragraph{Why this matters despite the paradox.}
In practice, the effective contamination level $\alpha$ is unknown and typically increases over time as web-scraped training corpora accumulate more machine-generated text.
A continuous monitoring dashboard would automatically trigger when $\alpha$ crosses the detectability threshold ($\alpha{\approx}0.50$), converting the paradox from a static limitation into a temporal advantage: the framework detects collapse precisely when contamination first becomes severe enough to matter.
The methodological contribution is independent of canary utility: the consensus framework and its three-pitfall diagnostic apply to any short-time-series lead-lag analysis in iterative training, regardless of which specific metrics are monitored.
The regime map itself is an actionable output: practitioners who know that $\alpha{<}0.25$ is below the detection floor should invest in data provenance and source filtering rather than metric monitoring at those contamination levels.

\paragraph{The prevention paradox under intervention.}
Effective intervention truncates the collapse trajectory that established Granger precedence in the first place: if an entropy-triggered intervention prevents diversity from declining, the statistical basis for the canary relationship no longer holds.
This is the epidemiological prevention paradox applied to training collapse: a successful canary eliminates the evidence of its own necessity.
Our intervention experiments (\S\ref{sec:intervention}), validated across two model scales (410M, 1.4B) and three seed-precision conditions, provide cross-scale evidence on how individual methods respond to this truncation.
Differenced cross-correlation retains significance under intervention (31/32 pairs significant), consistent with its sensitivity to local co-movement patterns that persist even in truncated trajectories.
Threshold onset detection, by contrast, fails entirely (0/8 pairs detected), because intervention prevents the sustained monotonic decline that this method requires.
These divergent responses reinforce the multi-method rationale of MMCT: no single method is robust across both observational and interventional settings, and the consensus framework's ability to weight methods by empirical reliability provides a natural path toward intervention-aware monitoring.
The practical implication is that once a canary triggers intervention, continued monitoring should rely on methods validated under truncated dynamics rather than those calibrated on unmitigated collapse.

\paragraph{Broader implications for training pipelines.}
In the Confirmatory regime ($\alpha{\geq}0.75$), the consensus framework can serve as a continuous monitoring signal within iterative training pipelines: the multi-method panel would run after each generation, and sustained agreement across metric pairs would flag potential collapse onset for human review.
Sequential monitoring experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:csmp}) reveal that null-calibrated CUSUM and simple calibrated thresholds yield equivalent detection times at all operating points tested, extending Claim~3 (method sensitivity) to the monitoring domain: even ostensibly more sophisticated sequential methods do not outperform calibrated baselines when the initial contamination signal is large relative to the allowance parameter.
The contribution of the monitoring framework lies in the null-calibration procedure (setting alarm thresholds from $\alpha{=}0.0$ data to guarantee FAR${=}$0\%) rather than in any specific test statistic.
The cost of running these tests per generation is negligible relative to training itself, though the practical utility paradox (\S\ref{sec:limitations}) and the scope of intervention validation (three seed-precision pairs across two model scales at $\alpha{=}1.0$, threshold confirmation at $\alpha{=}0.75$) mean that broader deployment---particularly to larger models and accumulate-mode training---requires further confirmation.
The 15\% entropy threshold would also trigger at $\alpha{=}0.60$ (generation~1 entropy drops 31.3\%), suggesting that the detection-and-cessation mechanism may extend below the Confirmatory regime; notably, the threshold trigger fires at $\alpha{=}0.60$ even though formal Granger detection fails at this level (synchronous collapse zone; \S\ref{sec:regime}), illustrating that magnitude-based triggers can complement temporal-precedence tests.
However, no intervention experiment was conducted at this contamination level, so efficacy at $\alpha{=}0.60$ remains unvalidated.

\paragraph{Token entropy versus perplexity.}
The finding that token entropy Granger-precedes diversity while perplexity does not ($F{\approx}0$, $p{=}0.99$ after differencing) requires clarification, since perplexity is the exponential of cross-entropy and appears mathematically related to token entropy.
The distinction lies in the evaluation domain: our ``token entropy'' is $H(p_\theta | \text{context})$ evaluated on \emph{held-out real data} (the model's predictive uncertainty on genuine text), while ``perplexity'' is $\exp(H_\text{cross})$ evaluated on \emph{model-generated text} (the model's self-consistency on its own outputs).
The identity $\text{ppl} = \exp(\text{entropy})$ holds only when the model distribution equals the data distribution, a condition that iterative collapse systematically violates.
In practice, both metrics trend downward during collapse (the model becomes more certain), producing high undifferenced correlation.
First-differencing removes this shared trend: the canary$\to$diversity channel survives because entropy \emph{leads} diversity decline by one generation (the model narrows its distribution before output diversity measurably falls), whereas the canary$\to$perplexity channel vanishes because entropy and perplexity co-move \emph{synchronously}, both driven by the same underlying distributional contraction.
Thus, the perplexity channel being ``spurious'' is not trivially expected from the mathematical relationship, but rather a substantive finding about collapse dynamics: the generation-evaluation divergence breaks the entropy--perplexity coupling in a temporally informative way.

\paragraph{NLP-specific constraints on lead-lag analysis.}
Our application of Granger-type methods to iterative training faces constraints absent in their original econometric settings.
First, observation length: typical econometric applications use $T{=}100$--$1000$ time points, whereas iterative training studies are limited to $T{=}5$--$20$ generations due to computational cost.
This severely constrains degrees of freedom for VAR-based methods; Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection (3--4/8) at $T{=}11$ reflects this constraint, as the augmentation order $d_{\max}$ consumes additional degrees of freedom (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
Second, non-stationarity is by design: each generation's training data differs from the previous generation's, making the underlying process non-stationary by construction rather than as an incidental property.
Standard stationarity tests (ADF, KPSS) may yield misleading results when applied to processes with deterministic degradation trajectories rather than stochastic unit roots.
Third, the sample-size bottleneck compounds with multiple testing: with only 8--32 pairs per regime, FDR correction operates on small multiplicity, limiting its ability to separate true from false discoveries.
These constraints motivate our multi-method consensus approach as a complement to, rather than replacement for, traditional significance testing.

\paragraph{Method sensitivity extends beyond parametric tests.}
We additionally tested Transfer Entropy (TE), a non-parametric information-theoretic alternative to Granger causality that makes no linearity assumptions.
TE produced 0/192 FDR-significant results across all conditions tested (12 runs $\times$ 8 pairs $\times$ forward/reverse, BH $q{=}0.05$), with TE--Granger concordance at 52.3\% (chance level).
This stands in sharp contrast to the parametric permutation Granger test, which identifies 6/8 FDR-significant forward pairs at $\alpha{=}1.0$.
The failure of TE at $T{=}11$ is consistent with known power limitations of non-parametric entropy estimators on short time series~\cite{schreiber2000measuring}, where binning discretization collapses distributional information that parametric models can still exploit.
This result extends Claim~3 beyond the five methods in our consensus panel: even the parametric vs.\ non-parametric distinction in analysis method can determine whether any signal is detected at all.

Change-point analysis under the null condition ($\alpha{=}0.00$) reveals that diversity metrics undergo structural breaks even without contamination, reflecting natural fine-tuning drift.
Our Granger analysis controls for this shared trend through first-differencing, which preserves canary$\to$downstream significance (24/24) while eliminating reverse-direction signal (0/8), confirming that the detected lead-lag relationship is specific to contamination-induced collapse rather than generic training dynamics (Appendix~\ref{app:change_point}).

\paragraph{Future work.}
Several directions extend this work.
Multivariate VAR models would enable testing for confounders and multi-directional Granger relationships beyond our current bivariate framework.
Multi-seed replication across the six validated architecture families would further strengthen the cross-architecture claims; evaluation on larger-scale models (${>}7$B parameters) remains an open direction.
Longer training runs ($T{\geq}20$ generations) could unlock threshold onset detection, which requires more generation-over-generation differences for $3\sigma$ calibration to achieve adequate power; longer runs could also improve Toda--Yamamoto's moderate detection rates by providing additional degrees of freedom for the augmented VAR (\S\ref{sec:ty_limitation}).
The SmolLM3 finding (ECE-only detection due to non-monotonic entropy) motivates systematic study of which canary metric is most reliable per architecture family.
Online monitoring, where canary metrics are computed within training pipelines for real-time collapse detection, is a natural applied extension.
Accumulate-mode experiments~\cite{dey2024breaking} would test whether canary dynamics differ from the replace-mode setting studied here.
Finally, connecting the empirically observed onset boundary ($\alpha{\approx}0.45$--$0.50$) to theoretical phase transition analysis~\cite{truong2025entropy} could yield a principled explanation for why canary signals emerge at this contamination regime rather than at lower contamination levels.

284	\subsection{Theoretical Motivation: Why Entropy Leads Diversity}
285	\label{sec:theory}
286	
287	The empirical lead-lag relationship between token entropy and lexical diversity (\S\ref{sec:regime}) admits a simple theoretical motivation grounded in the distinct mathematical properties of continuous and discrete summary statistics.
288	We present three arguments that, taken together, predict the observed temporal ordering and its dependence on contamination strength.
289	These arguments provide intuition rather than formal proof; the dose-response experiments in \S\ref{sec:regime} test the resulting predictions empirically.
290	
291	\paragraph{Continuous versus discrete response.}
292	Token entropy $H(p_t^{(g)}) = -\sum_v p_v \log p_v$ is a continuous functional of the token distribution $p_t^{(g)}$ at generation $g$: any infinitesimal shift in $p_t^{(g)}$ produces a proportional change in $H$.
293	Distinct-$n$ diversity $D_k^{(g)}$, by contrast, is a counting statistic.
294	An $n$-gram contributes to $D_k^{(g)}$ only when its probability exceeds an effective sampling threshold $\tau_n \approx 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of generated tokens.
295	Below $\tau_n$, the $n$-gram is absent from finite samples regardless of its true probability.
296	$D_k^{(g)}$ therefore responds to distributional change in discrete steps: it remains constant while probabilities drift within the interval above $\tau_n$, then drops abruptly when a probability crosses the threshold.
297	Because $H$ tracks every distributional perturbation while $D_k^{(g)}$ remains silent until a threshold crossing occurs, entropy is sensitive to distributional change strictly before diversity registers it.
298	
299	\paragraph{Four predicted detectability intervals.}
300	The continuous-versus-discrete asymmetry predicts four intervals of the contamination parameter $\alpha$, ordered by increasing signal strength:
301	\begin{enumerate}
302	\item \textbf{Blind spot} ($\alpha$ small).
303	The distributional shift is too weak for $H$ to exceed noise-level variation, and no $n$-gram probabilities cross $\tau_n$.
304	Both metrics show null response.
305	\item \textbf{Canary-only window} ($\alpha$ moderate-low).
306	$H$ registers a statistically significant shift, but the probability mass redistribution has not yet pushed enough $n$-grams below $\tau_n$ to alter $D_k^{(g)}$.
307	Entropy signals collapse; diversity does not.
308	\item \textbf{Lead-lag regime} ($\alpha$ moderate-high).
309	$H$ continues to lead, and $D_k^{(g)}$ begins to respond with a measurable delay as $n$-gram probabilities progressively cross $\tau_n$.
310	The temporal gap between the two is detectable by Granger-type tests.
311	\item \textbf{Synchronous collapse} ($\alpha$ high).
312	The distributional shift is so large that $H$ and $D_k^{(g)}$ change within the same generation, collapsing the lead to zero and rendering temporal precedence undetectable.
313	\end{enumerate}
314	These four intervals align with the empirical dose-response profile: a blind spot at $\alpha \leq 0.45$, onset of detection at $\alpha = 0.50$, reliable lead-lag at $\alpha \geq 0.75$, and a synchronous dip at $\alpha = 0.60$ where entropy and diversity shift near-simultaneously (\S\ref{sec:regime}).
315	We emphasize that this mapping is a qualitative prediction, not a quantitative derivation; the interval boundaries depend on model capacity, dataset properties, and sample size $N$.
316	
317	\paragraph{Connection to effective rank.}
318	The link between entropy and diversity can be made more concrete through the notion of effective rank~\texttt{[CITE]}.
319	For a probability distribution $P$, the effective rank $\mathrm{erank}(P) = \exp(H(P / \|P\|_1))$ measures the number of dimensions that carry substantial probability mass.
320	A decline in $H$ corresponds to a contraction of $\mathrm{erank}(P)$: the distribution concentrates on fewer tokens.
321	As concentration increases, tokens in the tail of $P$ fall below the sampling threshold $\tau_n$, and the $n$-grams they participate in vanish from generated text.

323	Entropy sits at the upstream end of this chain, which is why it responds first.
